--- title: "Distributional assumptions" description: "A count model assumes how widely counts scatter around its predictions. Simulating surveys from the fitted model shows whether it could have produced the real one, and a model that could not is sure of effects the data do not support." order: 2 categories: [assumptions] --- ## Every count model claims how widely counts scatter [Count regression](../03-supervised-learning/count-regression.qmd) fitted Poisson regression to the survey and found the counts varying more than Poisson allows. [Maximum likelihood](../04-how-algorithms-learn/maximum-likelihood.qmd) showed why that matters: the distribution a model assumes is what its fit is built on, and its standard errors come from it. This page adds a check that works for any model with a distribution, **simulating from the fitted model**, and shows what the wrong distribution costs: a model that is sure of an effect the data do not support. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## Each distribution ties the spread to the mean A model predicts an expected value at each station. Its distribution says how far the real values scatter around it, and for most distributions that scatter depends on the expected value itself. | Distribution | Variance at expected value μ | Used for | | --- | --- | --- | | Normal | The same everywhere | Linear regression | | Poisson | μ, the expected value itself | Poisson regression | | Negative binomial | μ + μ²/θ, more than Poisson | Counts of animals that gather in groups | | Bernoulli | μ(1 − μ), with μ a probability | Logistic regression, presence and absence | The choice is a claim about the animals. Poisson says that at a station expecting 4 animals, repeat hauls would vary with a standard deviation of 2. Animals that school or gather on patches of food vary far more than that, and the negative binomial's $\theta$ (theta) allows for it: the smaller $\theta$, the wider the scatter. ## Simulated surveys test a fitted model's distribution A fitted count model gives each station an expected count and a distribution around it. Drawing one random count for each station from that distribution gives a survey the model could have produced. Repeat that many times, and each simulated survey can be compared with the real one. The comparison needs a feature to count. Two are easy to read and matter to a biologist: the number of empty stations, and the largest catch. If the real survey's value sits far outside the range of the simulated ones, the model could not have produced the survey, whatever its predictions look like. ::: {.diagram} ![A fitted model gives each station an expected count and a distribution around it. Drawing a random count for every station, many times over, gives simulated surveys. A feature such as the number of empty stations is counted in each, and the real survey's value is compared with the range of simulated ones.](img/simulate.svg){fig-alt="Three cards. Fitted model, an expected count per station: bars of different heights for eight stations; the model gives each station an expected count and says how counts scatter. Simulated surveys, draw new counts many times: a grid of counts, one row for each of four surveys and one column for each station, with the zeros shaded, and the words and so on, 500 times. Compare, the real survey among them: a histogram of the number of empty stations in the simulated surveys, with a dashed line for the real survey far to its right; far outside means the model fails. A note says a model that could have produced the survey makes surveys that look like it."} ::: ## Worked example The data, the split by site and the recipe are those of [Count regression](../03-supervised-learning/count-regression.qmd): the survey's inputs, with squared depth and temperature, sand as the baseline seabed and spring as the baseline season. Poisson regression and the negative binomial model are fitted to the training stations. ### Preparing the data ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() split <- group_initial_split(survey, group = site_id, prop = 0.75) train <- training(split) curve_recipe <- recipe( abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 + salinity_psu + substrate + season, data = train ) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |> step_relevel(substrate, ref_level = "sand") |> step_poly(depth_m, temperature_c, degree = 2, options = list(raw = TRUE)) poisson_fit <- workflow(curve_recipe, poisson_reg()) |> fit(train) prepared <- prep(curve_recipe) nb_fit <- MASS::glm.nb(abundance ~ ., data = bake(prepared, new_data = NULL)) ``` ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd import statsmodels.api as sm from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.model_selection import GroupShuffleSplit from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, PolynomialFeatures from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() grouper = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, train_size=0.75, random_state=123) train_rows, test_rows = next(grouper.split(survey, groups=survey["site_id"])) train = survey.iloc[train_rows] categorical = ["substrate", "season"] predictors = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"] + categorical def squared(column): return (column, Pipeline([ ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("poly", PolynomialFeatures(degree=2, include_bias=False)), ]), [column]) curve_recipe = ColumnTransformer([ squared("depth_m"), squared("temperature_c"), ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), ["chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"]), ("categorical", OneHotEncoder(drop=["sand", "spring"], sparse_output=False), categorical), ]) prepared = curve_recipe.fit(train[predictors]) design = sm.add_constant(pd.DataFrame( prepared.transform(train[predictors]), columns=prepared.get_feature_names_out(), index=train.index)) poisson_fit = sm.GLM(train["abundance"], design, family=sm.families.Poisson()).fit() nb_fit = sm.NegativeBinomial(train["abundance"], design).fit( method="newton", disp=0) ``` ::: ::: ### Poisson regression makes far too few empty stations Each model's expected count at every training station is the starting point. The negative binomial also needs its $\theta$. Five hundred surveys are drawn from each model, and each is reduced to its number of empty stations and its largest catch. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} poisson_mean <- predict(poisson_fit, train)$.pred nb_mean <- fitted(nb_fit) simulate <- function(draw, times = 500) { map(seq_len(times), \(i) { counts <- draw() tibble(empty = sum(counts == 0), largest = max(counts)) }) |> list_rbind() } sims <- bind_rows( "Poisson regression" = simulate(\() rpois(nrow(train), poisson_mean)), "Negative binomial model" = simulate(\() rnbinom(nrow(train), mu = nb_mean, size = nb_fit$theta)), .id = "model" ) real <- tibble(feature = c("empty", "largest"), real = c(sum(train$abundance == 0), max(train$abundance))) # the middle 95% of the simulated surveys, beside the real one checks <- sims |> pivot_longer(c(empty, largest), names_to = "feature") |> summarise(low = quantile(value, 0.025), high = quantile(value, 0.975), .by = c(feature, model)) |> left_join(real, by = "feature") checks |> mutate(across(c(low, high), round)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|feature |model | low| high| real| |:-------|:-----------------------|---:|----:|----:| |empty |Poisson regression | 43| 67| 129| |largest |Poisson regression | 20| 35| 40| |empty |Negative binomial model | 108| 142| 129| |largest |Negative binomial model | 28| 88| 40|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} rng = np.random.default_rng(1) counts = train["abundance"].to_numpy() poisson_mean = poisson_fit.fittedvalues.to_numpy() nb_mean = nb_fit.predict(design).to_numpy() theta = 1 / nb_fit.params["alpha"] def simulate(draw, times=500): surveys = [draw() for _ in range(times)] return pd.DataFrame({"empty": [(s == 0).sum() for s in surveys], "largest": [s.max() for s in surveys]}) sims = pd.concat({ "Poisson regression": simulate(lambda: rng.poisson(poisson_mean)), "Negative binomial model": simulate( lambda: rng.negative_binomial(theta, theta / (theta + nb_mean))), }, names=["model"]).reset_index(level="model") real = {"empty": (counts == 0).sum(), "largest": counts.max()} # the middle 95% of the simulated surveys, beside the real one checks = (sims.melt(id_vars="model", var_name="feature") .groupby(["feature", "model"], sort=False)["value"] .quantile([0.025, 0.975]).unstack() .set_axis(["low", "high"], axis=1).reset_index()) checks["real"] = checks["feature"].map(real) checks.round() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | feature | model | low | high | real | |:----------|:------------------------|------:|-------:|-------:| | empty | Poisson regression | 48 | 72 | 133 | | empty | Negative binomial model | 111 | 144 | 133 | | largest | Poisson regression | 15 | 25 | 37 | | largest | Negative binomial model | 25 | 58 | 37 | ::: ::: ::: The training stations include 129 empty ones out of 598. Surveys simulated from Poisson regression have 43–67. Their largest catch runs from 20–35 animals, where the real survey's was 40. @fig-check shows the whole spread. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} check_plot <- function(which, x_label) { ggplot(sims, aes(.data[[which]], fill = model)) + geom_histogram(bins = 40, alpha = 0.7, position = "identity") + geom_vline(xintercept = real$real[real$feature == which], linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) + scale_fill_manual(values = c( "Poisson regression" = ml_palette[["vermilion"]], "Negative binomial model" = ml_palette[["blue"]])) + labs(x = x_label, y = "Simulated surveys", fill = NULL) } check_plot("empty", "Empty stations") + check_plot("largest", "Largest catch") + plot_layout(guides = "collect") & theme(legend.position = "bottom") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The number of empty stations and the largest catch in 500 surveys simulated from each fitted model, against the real survey (dashed). Poisson regression's surveys have far fewer empty stations and smaller largest catches than the real one. The negative binomial model's surveys contain the real values.](distributional-assumptions_files/figure-html/fig-check-1.png){#fig-check fig-alt='Two panels of overlapping histograms, one colour for surveys simulated from Poisson regression and one for the negative binomial model, with a dashed vertical line for the real survey. Left, empty stations: the Poisson histogram lies between about 43 and 67, far to the left of the real value of 129; the negative binomial histogram spreads from about 108 to 142 and contains it. Right, the largest catch: the Poisson histogram is narrow, ending near 35, with the real value of 40 at or beyond its edge; the negative binomial histogram is wide, with a long tail to the right, and contains the real value.' width=1600} ::: ::: ::: Poisson regression fails both checks. Its distribution allows too little scatter, so the counts stay near their expected values: few stations come up empty and none comes up very large. The real survey has both, because animals gather in groups. The negative binomial model passes: its surveys have 108–142 empty stations and a largest catch of 28–88, and the real survey sits inside both ranges. Both models predict much the same expected counts, as [Count regression](../03-supervised-learning/count-regression.qmd) found. The check tells them apart by their scatter, which the predictions alone never show. ## Poisson regression is sure of a summer effect the data do not support A distribution that allows too little scatter makes the model too sure of everything it estimates. The table below shows each seabed and season multiplier with its 95% confidence interval, as on [Count regression](../03-supervised-learning/count-regression.qmd). An interval that stays on one side of 1 says the data can tell that level from the baseline; this is the same as a *p*-value below 0.05. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} multipliers <- function(fitted) { tidy(fitted, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE) |> filter(str_detect(term, "substrate|season")) |> transmute(term = str_replace(term, "^(substrate|season)", "\\1: "), multiplier = estimate, conf_low = conf.low, conf_high = conf.high) } intervals <- bind_rows("Poisson regression" = multipliers(poisson_fit), "Negative binomial model" = multipliers(nb_fit), .id = "model") |> arrange(term) |> relocate(term) intervals |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|term |model | multiplier| conf_low| conf_high| |:-----------------|:-----------------------|----------:|--------:|---------:| |season: autumn |Poisson regression | 1.09| 0.96| 1.23| |season: autumn |Negative binomial model | 1.05| 0.81| 1.37| |season: summer |Poisson regression | 1.34| 1.07| 1.66| |season: summer |Negative binomial model | 1.31| 0.83| 2.07| |season: winter |Poisson regression | 0.87| 0.72| 1.05| |season: winter |Negative binomial model | 0.82| 0.56| 1.19| |substrate: gravel |Poisson regression | 1.15| 1.03| 1.29| |substrate: gravel |Negative binomial model | 1.21| 0.96| 1.54| |substrate: mud |Poisson regression | 1.34| 1.22| 1.47| |substrate: mud |Negative binomial model | 1.41| 1.16| 1.71| |substrate: rock |Poisson regression | 0.78| 0.65| 0.93| |substrate: rock |Negative binomial model | 0.89| 0.63| 1.29|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} def multipliers(fitted): interval = np.exp(fitted.conf_int()) table = pd.DataFrame({ "term": fitted.params.index.str.replace( r"^categorical__(substrate|season)_", r"\1: ", regex=True), "multiplier": np.exp(fitted.params).to_numpy(), "conf_low": interval[0].to_numpy(), "conf_high": interval[1].to_numpy(), }) keep = table["term"].str.contains("substrate|season") return table[keep].reset_index(drop=True) intervals = (pd.concat({"Poisson regression": multipliers(poisson_fit), "Negative binomial model": multipliers(nb_fit)}, names=["model"]) .reset_index(level="model") .sort_values("term", kind="stable") .reset_index(drop=True)) intervals[["term", "model", "multiplier", "conf_low", "conf_high"]].round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | term | model | multiplier | conf_low | conf_high | |:------------------|:------------------------|-------------:|-----------:|------------:| | season: autumn | Poisson regression | 1.18 | 1.03 | 1.35 | | season: autumn | Negative binomial model | 1.15 | 0.86 | 1.53 | | season: summer | Poisson regression | 2.19 | 1.73 | 2.76 | | season: summer | Negative binomial model | 2.08 | 1.27 | 3.39 | | season: winter | Poisson regression | 0.64 | 0.52 | 0.79 | | season: winter | Negative binomial model | 0.62 | 0.41 | 0.94 | | substrate: gravel | Poisson regression | 1.14 | 1.01 | 1.3 | | substrate: gravel | Negative binomial model | 1.17 | 0.91 | 1.5 | | substrate: mud | Poisson regression | 1.37 | 1.24 | 1.52 | | substrate: mud | Negative binomial model | 1.36 | 1.12 | 1.66 | | substrate: rock | Poisson regression | 0.73 | 0.59 | 0.89 | | substrate: rock | Negative binomial model | 0.72 | 0.5 | 1.04 | ::: ::: ::: Under Poisson regression, summer stations hold 1.34 times the count of spring ones, with an interval from 1.07 to 1.66. Taken at face value, the data show a summer effect beyond what temperature and chlorophyll explain. The negative binomial model's estimate is close, 1.31, but its interval runs from 0.83 to 2.07 and includes 1: allowing for the real scatter, the data cannot tell summer from spring. Averaged over the coefficients, its standard errors are 2.0 times Poisson regression's. The negative binomial model has it right. The simulation gave season no effect of its own: season changes the water's temperature and chlorophyll, and both are already in the model. A report built on Poisson regression would have described a seasonal effect that is not there, and nothing in its predictions or its coefficients would have warned of it. Honest intervals have a price. The simulation did make rocky ground poorer for the species, and Poisson regression's interval for rock, 0.65 to 0.93, stays below 1. The negative binomial model's, 0.63 to 1.29, does not, as [Count regression](../03-supervised-learning/count-regression.qmd) found. Gravel, which the simulation made a little richer, goes the same way. Allowing for the scatter, this many stations cannot pin these effects down; that is what the data support. ## A passed check is not a correct model The negative binomial model passed both checks, but a check only tests the features it counts. Three limits follow. - **Choose features that matter to the question.** Empty stations matter for where a species occurs, the largest catch for how much it can aggregate. A species absent from part of the shelf can have more empty stations than even a negative binomial makes; models with a separate part for presence and absence exist for that case. - **The simulation treats every station as independent.** Each count is drawn on its own, yet stations at the same site share their water and seabed. The negative binomial's intervals rest on that independence too, so they may still be too narrow; [Independence of observations](independence-of-observations.qmd) measures by how much. - **Extra scatter can be missing structure.** A missing input, or a curve the model cannot bend to, leaves scatter that the negative binomial will absorb into $\theta$. [Maximum likelihood](../04-how-algorithms-learn/maximum-likelihood.qmd) asked its readers to add temperature and watch $\theta$ change. Improve the expected counts first, then judge the scatter that remains. ## Models without a distribution still assume a spread A random forest or a boosted model states no distribution, so it cannot be simulated from and gives no confidence intervals. The assumption has not gone; it has moved into the loss. Squared error is the loss that the Normal distribution gives, as [Maximum likelihood](../04-how-algorithms-learn/maximum-likelihood.qmd) showed, and it treats a miss of 10 animals at a station expecting 30 as just as bad as one at a station expecting 2. For counts whose spread grows with their size, a Poisson loss, which tree ensembles such as `xgboost` also offer, matches the data better. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - A distribution says how widely real values scatter around the expected value. Poisson says the variance equals the expected count; animals that gather in groups vary more. - **Simulating from the fitted model** tests that claim: draw many surveys from the model and see whether the real one looks like them. - Surveys from Poisson regression had 43–67 empty stations against 129 in the real one. The negative binomial model's contained the real survey's empty stations and largest catch. - Poisson regression was sure of a summer effect that the simulation never put there; the negative binomial model's wider intervals were not. They could no longer tell rock from sand either, which is what the data support. - A passed check tests only the features it counts, and the simulation assumes every station is independent. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Add a third feature to `simulate()`: the number of stations catching exactly one animal. Does the negative binomial model pass that check too? 2. Fit `linear_reg()` with `curve_recipe` and simulate from it with `rnorm()`, using its predictions as the mean and `sigma()` of its fitted engine as the standard deviation. How many stations per simulated survey get a count below zero?
